stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is (9x − 490)°. The sum of the measures of one of the acute angles and three of the obtuse angles is (−18x + w)°. What is the value of w?
whyCorrect: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, every acute angle is congruent to every other acute angle and every obtuse angle is supplementary to them. So each obtuse angle measures 180 − (9x − 490). One acute plus three obtuse is (9x − 490) + 3[180 − (9x − 490)] = 540 − 2(9x − 490) = 540 − 18x + 980 = 1520 − 18x. Matching that to −18x + w gives w = 1520. Notice you never need x itself — the −18x on both sides is the signal that the x-terms are meant to cancel.

stem: In isosceles triangle ABC, sides AB and AC are congruent. Point D divides side BC such that the length of BD is \(\frac{4}{7}\) of the length of BC. Point E lies on side AB and point F lies on side AC such that when segments DE and DF are drawn, angle BED is congruent to angle CFD. If the length of BE is 8, what is the length of CF?
whyCorrect: Because AB and AC are congruent, the base angles satisfy angle B = angle C. You are also told angle BED = angle CFD. Two pairs of congruent angles give triangle BED ~ triangle CFD, with B matching C, E matching F and D matching D. Since BD is \(\frac{4}{7}\) of BC, CD is \(\frac{3}{7}\) of BC, so the ratio of similarity is BD : CD = 4 : 3. Then BE : CF = 4 : 3, and CF = 8 × \(\frac{3}{4}\) = 6.

whyWrong.B: This comes from adding rather than scaling — 8 + 6, or treating the 4 : 3 split as something to add onto the given length. The similar triangles give a multiplicative relationship, not an additive one.
whyWrong.C: This is 8 × 4, using the numerator of \(\frac{4}{7}\) as the scale factor. The scale factor is BD : CD = 4 : 3, not 4 : 1, and it must shrink BE, not enlarge it.
whyWrong.D: This is 8 × 7, using the whole of BC against BD. The triangle containing CF sits on CD, which is \(\frac{3}{7}\) of BC, not on BC itself.

stem: The perimeter of an isosceles right triangle is \(52+52\sqrt{2}\) inches. What is the length, in inches, of the hypotenuse of this triangle?
whyCorrect: An isosceles right triangle with leg \(a\) has hypotenuse \(a\sqrt{2}\), so its perimeter is \(2a+a\sqrt{2}=a(2+\sqrt{2})\). Set that equal to \(52+52\sqrt{2}=52(1+\sqrt{2})\) and solve: \(a=\frac{52(1+\sqrt{2})}{2+\sqrt{2}}\). Multiply top and bottom by \(2-\sqrt{2}\); the denominator becomes 2 and the numerator becomes \(52\sqrt{2}\), so \(a=26\sqrt{2}\). The hypotenuse is \(a\sqrt{2}=26\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}=52\). The trap is that the perimeter is written to look like it splits as leg + leg + hypotenuse; it does not.

whyWrong.A: This is half of 52, which would be the answer if you read the perimeter's first term, 52, as the sum of the two legs. The two parts of \(52+52\sqrt{2}\) are not the legs and the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.B: This is the leg length \(a\), the value you get partway through. The question asks for the hypotenuse, which is \(a\sqrt{2}\).
whyWrong.D: This treats the \(52\sqrt{2}\) term of the perimeter as the hypotenuse directly. If it were, the two legs would sum to 52, making each leg 26 and the hypotenuse \(26\sqrt{2}\), which contradicts the assumption.

stem: The line segment shown in the xy-plane represents one of the legs of a right triangle. The area of this triangle is \(48\sqrt{13}\) square units. What is the length, in units, of the other leg of this triangle?
whyCorrect: First get the length of the drawn leg from its endpoints with the distance formula: the horizontal change is 9 and the vertical change is 6, so the length is \(\sqrt{9^{2}+6^{2}}=\sqrt{117}=3\sqrt{13}\). For a right triangle the two legs are the base and the height, so \(\frac{1}{2}(3\sqrt{13})(L)=48\sqrt{13}\). Multiply by 2 and divide by \(3\sqrt{13}\): \(L=\frac{96\sqrt{13}}{3\sqrt{13}}=32\). The \(\sqrt{13}\) cancels entirely, which is the sign you set it up correctly.

whyWrong.A: This is what you get if you write the area as (leg)(leg) instead of \(\frac{1}{2}\)(leg)(leg) — it is exactly half of the right answer.
whyWrong.C: This is the length of the leg already drawn, not the other one.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the drawn leg. Doubling is not what the area equation asks for; you have to divide the doubled area by the drawn leg, and the radical cancels when you do.

note: Figure needed: a line segment in the xy-plane from (-5, 3) to (4, 9), drawn on a grid with x from -8 to 8 and y from 0 to 16.

stem: A right circular cone has a volume of \(2{,}700\pi\) cubic centimeters and the area of its base is \(225\pi\) square centimeters. What is the slant height, in centimeters, of this cone?
whyCorrect: The base area gives the radius: \(\pi r^{2}=225\pi\), so \(r=15\). Now use \(V=\frac{1}{3}(\text{base area})h\): \(\frac{1}{3}(225\pi)h=2{,}700\pi\), so \(75h=2{,}700\) and \(h=36\). The slant height is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the radius and the height: \(\sqrt{15^{2}+36^{2}}=\sqrt{1{,}521}=39\). The last step is the one students skip — slant height is not the height.

whyWrong.A: This is \(2{,}700\div225\), which drops the \(\frac{1}{3}\) from the cone volume formula. Including it gives a height of 36, not 12.
whyWrong.B: This is the radius, an intermediate value.
whyWrong.C: This is the vertical height of the cone. The slant height runs along the surface from the apex to the edge of the base, so it is the hypotenuse of the triangle with legs 15 and 36 and is longer than 36.

stem: A property owner wants to find the length \(x\), in feet, across a pond as represented in the figure. PR intersects ST at point Q, and angle PTQ is congruent to angle RSQ. The lengths represented by PQ, TQ, QS, and RS were determined to be 4,200 feet, 8,400 feet, 1,400 feet, and 1,600 feet, respectively. What is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Angles PQT and RQS are vertical angles, so they are congruent, and you are told angle PTQ is congruent to angle RSQ. That makes triangle PTQ similar to triangle RSQ, with P matching R, T matching S, and Q matching Q. The scale factor comes from the pair of corresponding sides you know completely: TQ : SQ = 8,400 : 1,400 = 6. The distance across the pond is PT, which corresponds to RS, so \(x = 6 \times 1{,}600 = 9{,}600\) feet.
note: Figure needed: two segments PR and ST crossing at Q. T is below P on the left (PT spans the pond, labelled x, drawn as a lens/oval shape); S is upper right and R is lower right, so PR runs from upper left down to lower right and ST runs from lower left up to upper right, crossing at Q.

stem: A right square pyramid has a surface area of 75,264 square inches, which includes a base area of 36,864 square inches. What is the slant height, in inches, of this pyramid?
whyCorrect: The base is a square of area 36,864, so its side is \(\sqrt{36{,}864}=192\) inches. Subtract the base from the total to get the lateral area: 75,264 − 36,864 = 38,400 square inches. That lateral area is four congruent triangles, each with base 192 and height equal to the slant height \(\ell\), so \(4\cdot\frac{1}{2}(192)\ell = 384\ell = 38{,}400\). Therefore \(\ell = 100\) inches.

stem: The volume of a right rectangular prism with a square base is 2,448 cubic centimeters. If the area of the square base is 144 square centimeters, what is the area, in square centimeters, of one of the four lateral faces of the prism?
whyCorrect: Volume = (base area)(height), so the height is 2,448 ÷ 144 = 17 cm. The square base has area 144, so each side is \(\sqrt{144}=12\) cm. A single lateral face is a rectangle whose sides are one base edge and the height: 12 × 17 = 204 square centimeters. The trap is stopping at the height or reporting all four faces at once.

whyWrong.A: This is the height of the prism, 2,448 ÷ 144. You still have to multiply it by the 12 cm base edge to get a face's area.
whyWrong.C: No step here produces 540. If you got it, check that you divided the volume by the base area (144) to get the height, not by the base edge or the perimeter.
whyWrong.D: This is the combined area of all four lateral faces, 4 × 204. The question asks for one of them.

stem: A right square pyramid has a height of 11 centimeters (cm). A second right square pyramid has a height of 22 centimeters. The area of the bases of each of the two pyramids is 100 cm<sup>2</sup>. Which of the following is closest to the difference in the surface area of the second pyramid and the surface area of the first pyramid, in cm<sup>2</sup>?
whyCorrect: Each base is a square of area 100, so each base edge is 10 cm and the two bases cancel out of the difference — only the lateral areas differ. The slant height of a right square pyramid is \(\sqrt{h^{2}+\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)^{2}}\), using half the base edge, so the slant heights are \(\sqrt{11^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{146}\approx 12.083\) and \(\sqrt{22^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{509}\approx 22.561\). Lateral area is \(4\cdot\frac{1}{2}(10)\ell = 20\ell\), so the difference is \(20(22.561-12.083)\approx 209.6\), closest to 209.

whyWrong.B: This is what you get by using the pyramid's height, 11 and 22, directly as the slant height: 20(22 − 11) = 220. The slant height runs up the middle of a triangular face and is always longer than the vertical height.
whyWrong.C: This is the difference in volumes, \(\frac{1}{3}(100)(22-11)\approx 366.7\), not surface areas.
whyWrong.D: This is the surface area of the second pyramid on its own, \(100+20\sqrt{509}\approx 551\). You still have to subtract the first pyramid's surface area.

stem: In the figure, parallel lines r and s are intersected by lines t, u, and w. If d = 42, g = 143, and h > d, which statement about j and p must be true?
whyCorrect: Work with the angle each slanted line makes with the horizontal parallel lines. Because r and s are parallel, the angle a line makes at r is the same angle it makes at s, so h describes the tilt of line u and d describes the tilt of line w, while g describes the tilt of line t. Where two slanted lines meet, the angle between them is the difference of their tilts: \(j = g - h = 143 - h\) and \(p = g - d = 143 - 42 = 101\). Since h > 42, subtracting h takes away more than subtracting 42 does, so \(j \lt 101 = p\).

whyWrong.A: This would require h = d. You are told h > d, which is exactly the condition that forces the two angles apart.
whyWrong.B: p is already 101 on its own, so \(j+p\) cannot be 90 for any positive j.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the inequality. A larger h means a steeper line u relative to t, which makes the angle between them smaller, not larger.

note: Figure needed: horizontal parallel lines r (upper) and s (lower). Line t descends steeply left-to-right, line u ascends steeply left-to-right, and they cross above r with angle j marked in the upward-opening region between them. g is marked at t's intersection with r, in the region above r and right of t. h is marked at u's intersection with s, above s and right of u. Line w ascends left-to-right on the right side; d is marked at its intersection with r, above r and right of w. Lines t and w cross below s, with p marked in the downward-opening region between them.

stem: A right triangular pyramid has exactly six edges. Each of these edges is 96 centimeters long. If the surface area of the pyramid is \(k\sqrt{3}\) square centimeters, what is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Six edges all of the same length means all four faces are congruent equilateral triangles — a regular tetrahedron, so the base counts as a face too. An equilateral triangle of side \(s\) has area \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^{2}\), so one face is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(96)^{2}=\frac{9216\sqrt{3}}{4}=2304\sqrt{3}\). Four of them give \(9216\sqrt{3}\), so k = 9216. The common slip is counting only the three slanted faces and getting 6,912.

stem: A right rectangular prism has a base area of 28p square centimeters (cm<sup>2</sup>). The length of the base of the rectangular prism is 12 cm, and the height of the rectangular prism is 4 cm. Which expression represents the surface area, in cm<sup>2</sup>, of the right rectangular prism?
whyCorrect: Get the width first: base area = length × width, so \(w=\frac{28p}{12}=\frac{7p}{3}\). Surface area is \(2(\ell w)+2(\ell h)+2(wh)\). The top and bottom give \(2(28p)=56p\); the two faces measuring 12 by 4 give \(2(48)=96\); the two faces measuring \(\frac{7p}{3}\) by 4 give \(2\cdot\frac{28p}{3}=\frac{56p}{3}\). Adding, \(56p+\frac{56p}{3}=\frac{168p+56p}{3}=\frac{224p}{3}\), so the total is \(\frac{224p}{3}+96\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(\frac{224p}{3}+96p\) collected into one fraction. The 96 comes from the two 12-by-4 faces, whose dimensions contain no p, so it must stay a constant.
whyWrong.C: This treats both pairs of side faces as 12 by 4, giving 4(48) = 192, which assumes the base is a square of side 12. Only one pair of side faces has the 12 cm edge; the other pair uses the width \(\frac{7p}{3}\).
whyWrong.D: The constant 96 is right but the p-term is far too big. It comes from multiplying by the base area 28p again rather than dividing it by the 12 cm length to find the width.

Cylinder B\(4{,}608\pi\)
The table shows the volume of two similar solids, right circular cylinder A and right circular cylinder B. The radius of right circular cylinder A is 3 units. The surface area of right circular cylinder A is \(k\pi\) square units, and the surface area of right circular cylinder B is \(n\pi\) square units, where k and n are constants. What is the value of \(n-k\)? (The surface area of a right circular cylinder with radius r and height h is \(2\pi r^{2}+2\pi rh\).)
whyCorrect: Cylinder A first: \(\pi(3)^{2}h=72\pi\) gives h = 8, so its surface area is \(2\pi(9)+2\pi(3)(8)=18\pi+48\pi=66\pi\) and k = 66. For similar solids the volumes scale as the cube of the linear ratio, so \(\frac{4{,}608\pi}{72\pi}=64\) means the linear ratio is \(\sqrt[3]{64}=4\). Areas scale as the square of that ratio, \(4^{2}=16\), so \(n=16(66)=1{,}056\). Then \(n-k=1{,}056-66=990\). The step people miss is that the area ratio is 16, not 64.

stem: \[x^{2}-6x+y^{2}-12y-36=0\]In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle. If this circle is inscribed in a square, what is the perimeter of the square?
whyCorrect: Complete the square in both variables: \(x^{2}-6x\) needs +9 and \(y^{2}-12y\) needs +36, so the equation becomes \((x-3)^{2}+(y-6)^{2}=36+9+36=81\). The radius is \(\sqrt{81}=9\). A circle inscribed in a square touches all four sides, so the side of the square equals the diameter, 18. The perimeter is 4(18) = 72.

whyWrong.A: This is the side length of the square (the diameter of the circle), not the perimeter. Multiply by 4.
whyWrong.B: This is 4 times the radius. Each side of the square is the full diameter, 18, not the radius 9.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the correct perimeter, which happens if you take each side of the square to be twice the diameter instead of equal to it.

stem: \[(x+3)^{2}+(y-18)^{2}=169\]The graph of the given equation is a circle in the xy-plane. The point (a, b) lies on the circle. Which of the following is a possible value for a?
whyCorrect: The circle has center (-3, 18) and radius \(\sqrt{169}=13\), so the x-coordinate of any point on it satisfies \(-3-13 \le a \le -3+13\), that is \(-16 \le a \le 10\). Every one of -16, -10, 3 and 10 falls in that interval, so all four are possible values of a; only 16 lies outside the circle's horizontal reach. As printed, the question has four correct answers.
note: DEFECTIVE as printed. Five choices are given (A-E, itself non-standard) and four of them - -16, -10, 3 and 10 - are all possible x-coordinates, since a can be anything in [-16, 10]. Only E (16) is impossible. Either the choices need replacing (the real SAT version would offer one value inside [-16, 10] and three outside) or the stem should read 'which is NOT a possible value', in which case the answer is E. No answer recorded because there is no unique one.

stem: \[x^{2}-16x+y^{2}-10y-55=0\]In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle. If this circle is inscribed in a square, what is the perimeter of the square?
whyCorrect: Complete the square: \(x^{2}-16x\) needs +64 and \(y^{2}-10y\) needs +25, giving \((x-8)^{2}+(y-5)^{2}=55+64+25=144\). The radius is 12, so the diameter is 24. An inscribed circle touches all four sides of the square, so the square's side is that diameter, 24, and the perimeter is 4(24) = 96.

whyWrong.A: This is the side of the square (the diameter), not its perimeter.
whyWrong.B: This is 4 times the radius. The side of the square is the diameter 24, not the radius 12.
whyWrong.D: This is 4(55), using the constant term of the equation as though it were a length. That 55 has to be moved across and combined with the 64 and 25 from completing the square before you have \(r^{2}\).

stem: A circle in the xy-plane has a diameter with endpoints (a, 11) and (a, d), where a and d are constants. An equation of this circle is \((x-a)^{2}+(y-17)^{2}=r^{2}\), where r is a positive constant. What is the value of d?
whyCorrect: The equation shows the center is (a, 17). The center of a circle is the midpoint of any diameter, so \(\frac{11+d}{2}=17\), giving \(11+d=34\) and d = 23. Equivalently, 17 is 6 above 11, so the other endpoint must be 6 above 17.

whyWrong.A: This goes 6 units the wrong way from 11. The center at 17 is above the endpoint at 11, so the other endpoint has to be above the center, not below the first endpoint.
whyWrong.B: This is the length of the diameter, 23 - 11 = 12, not the coordinate of the endpoint.
whyWrong.C: This is the y-coordinate of the center. The center lies between the two endpoints; it is not one of them.

stem: In the xy-plane, a unit circle with center at the origin O contains point A with coordinates (1, 0) and point B with coordinates \(\left(\frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}, -\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\right)\). If the measure of angle AOB is p radians, what is the value of \(\frac{\cos p}{\sin p}\)?
whyCorrect: Angle AOB is the angle at the origin between the ray toward (1, 0) and the ray toward B. Its measure is a positive number, so p is the size of that opening, \(p=\arctan\!\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)\), regardless of B sitting below the x-axis. Building the right triangle from B's coordinates, the leg along the x-axis is \(\frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}\) and the leg perpendicular to it is \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\) on a unit hypotenuse, so \(\cos p=\frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}\) and \(\sin p=\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\). The \(\sqrt{34}\) cancels in the quotient, leaving \(\frac{5}{3}\).
note: Ambiguous as printed, and worth a human decision. Read strictly - 'the measure of angle AOB' is a geometric angle measure, so it is positive and sin p > 0 - the answer is 5/3. If the book instead intends B to be the terminal point of an angle in standard position, so that B = (cos p, sin p) with sin p negative, the answer is -5/3. I have recorded 5/3 because an angle measure cannot be negative, but the printed key is likely -5/3. Question 53 on the same page does not have this problem because its point B lies above the x-axis, where the two readings agree.

stem: In the xy-plane, a unit circle with center at the origin O contains point A with coordinates (1, 0) and point B with coordinates \(\left(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{89}}, \frac{8}{\sqrt{89}}\right)\). If the measure of angle AOB is w radians, what is the value of \(\tan w\)?
whyCorrect: On a unit circle centered at the origin, a point reached by rotating the ray toward (1, 0) through w radians has coordinates \((\cos w, \sin w)\). Here B lies above the x-axis, so w is between 0 and \(\pi\) and the geometric angle AOB is exactly that rotation: \(\cos w=-\frac{5}{\sqrt{89}}\) and \(\sin w=\frac{8}{\sqrt{89}}\). Then \(\tan w=\frac{\sin w}{\cos w}=\frac{8/\sqrt{89}}{-5/\sqrt{89}}=-\frac{8}{5}\). Do not drop the sign - B is in the second quadrant, where tangent is negative.

Cylinder B\(3{,}024\pi\)
The table shows the volume of two similar solids, right circular cylinder A and right circular cylinder B. The radius of right circular cylinder A is 4 units. The surface area of right circular cylinder A is \(k\pi\) square units, and the surface area of right circular cylinder B is \(n\pi\) square units, where k and n are constants. What is the value of \(n-k\)? (The surface area of a right circular cylinder with radius r and height h is \(2\pi r^{2}+2\pi rh\).)
whyCorrect: Start with cylinder A: \(\pi(4)^{2}h=112\pi\) gives h = 7, so its surface area is \(2\pi(16)+2\pi(4)(7)=32\pi+56\pi=88\pi\) and k = 88. For similar solids the volume ratio is the cube of the linear ratio: \(\frac{3{,}024\pi}{112\pi}=27\), so the linear ratio is \(\sqrt[3]{27}=3\). Surface areas scale by the square of that, \(3^{2}=9\), so \(n=9(88)=792\) and \(n-k=792-88=704\). Do not scale the area by 27; that is the volume factor.

stem: A right rectangular prism has a base of 28p square centimeters (cm<sup>2</sup>). The length of the base of the rectangular prism is 12 cm, and the height of the rectangular prism is 4 cm. Which expression represents the surface area, in cm<sup>2</sup>, of the right rectangular prism?
whyCorrect: The base area is length times width, so \(w=\frac{28p}{12}=\frac{7p}{3}\). Add the three pairs of faces: top and bottom give \(2(28p)=56p\); the two faces measuring 12 by 4 give \(2(48)=96\); the two faces measuring \(\frac{7p}{3}\) by 4 give \(2\cdot\frac{28p}{3}=\frac{56p}{3}\). Combine the p-terms over a common denominator: \(56p+\frac{56p}{3}=\frac{224p}{3}\), giving \(\frac{224p}{3}+96\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(\frac{224p}{3}+96p\) written as one fraction. The 96 comes from the two 12-by-4 faces, whose dimensions contain no p, so it cannot pick up a factor of p.
whyWrong.C: This uses 12 by 4 for all four side faces, giving 4(48) = 192, which would only be right if the base were a square of side 12. Only one pair of side faces uses the 12 cm edge; the other pair uses the width \(\frac{7p}{3}\).
whyWrong.D: The 96 is right but the p-term is far too large. It comes from multiplying by the base area 28p again instead of dividing it by 12 to get the width.

note: The book prints the first words as 'A right triangular prism has a base of 28p square centimeters', then calls it a rectangular prism in every following sentence and asks for the surface area of a right rectangular prism. Transcribed as 'right rectangular prism'; 'triangular' is a typo. Note also that this question is a verbatim duplicate of Geometry #46 on page 54 (same numbers, same four choices) - only one of the two should be banked.

stem: \[2x^{2}+2y^{2}+tx+ty-78=0\]The given equation, where t is a positive constant, defines a circle in the xy-plane. The radius of this circle is \(\sqrt{41}\). What is the value of t?
whyCorrect: Divide through by 2 first so the squared terms have coefficient 1: \(x^{2}+y^{2}+\frac{t}{2}x+\frac{t}{2}y-39=0\). Completing the square on each variable adds \(\left(\frac{t}{4}\right)^{2}\) twice, giving \(\left(x+\frac{t}{4}\right)^{2}+\left(y+\frac{t}{4}\right)^{2}=39+\frac{t^{2}}{8}\). Set that equal to \(r^{2}=41\): \(\frac{t^{2}}{8}=2\), so \(t^{2}=16\) and, since t is positive, t = 4. Skipping the division by 2 is the usual mistake - completing the square only works once the leading coefficients are 1.

stem: The figure shows a rectangular pool surrounded by a concrete path that is x feet (ft) wide on all sides. The pool is 21 ft long and 13 ft wide. The area of the concrete path is 240 ft<sup>2</sup>. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: The path adds x to each of the four sides, so the outer rectangle is \((21+2x)\) by \((13+2x)\) - the width is added twice to each dimension, not once. The path is the outer rectangle minus the pool: \((21+2x)(13+2x)-21(13)=240\), so \((21+2x)(13+2x)=513\). Expanding gives \(4x^{2}+68x+273=513\), or \(x^{2}+17x-60=0\), which factors as \((x-3)(x+20)=0\). A width must be positive, so x = 3.

whyWrong.B: This is 2x, the total amount added to each dimension of the pool, not the width of the path itself.
whyWrong.C: This is the other root of the quadratic with its sign flipped. \(x=-20\) solves the equation algebraically but a path cannot have negative width, so it is rejected.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the rejected root, combining both errors above - the negative solution kept, then multiplied by 2.

note: Figure needed: a shaded rectangle (the concrete path) with a smaller unshaded rectangle labelled 'Pool' centred inside it, and a vertical segment from the top of the outer rectangle to the top of the pool labelled 'x ft'. All dimensions are given in the stem, so the figure is illustrative.

stem: Two isosceles triangles are shown above. If 180 − z = 3y and y = 50, what is the value of x?
whyCorrect: The angles of the right-hand triangle sum to 180, and its two tick-marked sides are congruent, so its two base angles are equal and together they measure \(180-z\). You are handed that quantity directly: \(180-z=3y=3(50)=150\), so each base angle is 75. The angle marked x is not that base angle - it sits on the other side of the slanted segment, between the segment and the upward continuation of the vertical line, so it is the base angle's supplement: \(x=180-75=105\). You never need z or the left-hand triangle at all.
note: Figure needed, and the answer turns on one detail of it. Two vertical lines bound the figure. Four segments meet at a single point between them: two run left to the left-hand vertical line (marked with single ticks, forming the left isosceles triangle with apex angle y inside), two run right to the right-hand vertical line (marked with double ticks, forming the right isosceles triangle with apex angle z inside). The label x sits ABOVE the upper right-hand segment and to the LEFT of the right vertical line, i.e. in the wedge between that segment and the part of the vertical line running upward past the vertex - so x is the EXTERIOR angle there, 105, not the interior base angle, 75. If the printed key is 75, the disagreement is over exactly this label placement. Also note the four segments bend at the shared point (the upper-left segment does not continue as the lower-right one), so y and z are not vertical angles and there is no contradiction with y = 50.

stem: The solid in the figure is the shaded part of a cone with a height of 10 cm obtained by cutting its top parallel to the base, 10 cm from its tip. The volume of the solid is
whyCorrect: The shaded solid is a frustum: the whole cone (radius 3, height 20) with the small top cone (radius 1.5, height 10) removed. Work with the difference rather than memorising a frustum formula: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^{2}(20)-\frac{1}{3}\pi(1.5)^{2}(10)=60\pi-7.5\pi=52.5\pi\). That evaluates to about 164.93 cubic centimeters. The check that the setup is right is that the small cone is similar to the big one - half the radius and half the height.

whyWrong.A: \(60\pi\) is the volume of the entire cone, before the top is cut off. You still have to remove the small cone.
whyWrong.B: \(7.5\pi\) is the volume of the small cone that was cut away, not the piece that remains.
whyWrong.D: This is not produced by any correct route; it is close enough to the answer to look plausible. If you got it, check that you used the full cone's height of 20, not 10, and subtracted the small cone rather than averaging the two radii.

note: Figure needed: a cone standing point-up, total height 20 marked on the right, the top 10 cm marked on the left, a horizontal cut 10 cm from the tip where the radius is 1.5, and a base radius of 3. The frustum below the cut is shaded. The radii 1.5 and 3 appear only in the figure, so the question is unanswerable without it.

stem: The area of an isosceles right triangle inscribed in a circle with center at O and radius \(5\sqrt{2}\) is
whyCorrect: An angle inscribed in a circle is a right angle exactly when it opens onto a diameter, so the hypotenuse of this triangle is a diameter: \(2(5\sqrt{2})=10\sqrt{2}\). In an isosceles right triangle the hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{2}\) times a leg, so each leg is \(\frac{10\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}=10\). The legs are perpendicular, so they serve as base and height: area \(=\frac{1}{2}(10)(10)=50\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(10\times10\), the product of the two legs with the \(\frac{1}{2}\) left out.
whyWrong.C: This is the length of the hypotenuse (the diameter), not an area.
whyWrong.D: This uses one leg of 10 with the radius \(5\sqrt{2}\) as the other dimension. The radius is not a side of the triangle; both legs are 10.
whyWrong.E: This uses the hypotenuse \(10\sqrt{2}\) as if it were a leg: \(\frac{1}{2}(10\sqrt{2})(10)\). Only the two legs are perpendicular, so only they can be the base and height.

note: The book prints five choices, A-E, rather than the standard four.

stem: In the xy-plane, a circle has center C with coordinates (p, 8), where p is a constant. Points G and H lie on the circle. Point G has coordinates \((p+3\sqrt{5},\, 14)\), and point H has coordinates (q, 8), where q is a constant greater than p. What is the area, in square units, of triangle CGH?
whyCorrect: Find the radius from G: it sits \(3\sqrt{5}\) to the right of the center and 6 above it, so \(r=\sqrt{(3\sqrt{5})^{2}+6^{2}}=\sqrt{45+36}=\sqrt{81}=9\). The radical disappears, which is the whole point of the numbers chosen. H has the same y-coordinate as the center, so it is 9 units horizontally from C, and since q > p it is at \((p+9,\,8)\). Take CH as the base: it is horizontal with length 9, and G is 14 − 8 = 6 units above that line, so the area is \(\frac{1}{2}(9)(6)=27\).

whyWrong.A: This carries a stray \(\sqrt{5}\) from G's coordinate into the answer. Once you square \(3\sqrt{5}\) to get 45 and add 36, the radius is the whole number 9 and no radical survives.
whyWrong.C: \(5\sqrt{27}=15\sqrt{3}\approx 25.98\), which is close enough to 27 to look right but is not it. It comes from swapping the 5 and the 27 inside the radical rather than computing the base and height.
whyWrong.D: This attaches a \(\sqrt{6}\) to the correct value 27, taking the height 6 from under a radical it was never under. The height is exactly 6 units, the difference of the y-coordinates.

stem: In the xy-plane, the line y = 3x − 14 is tangent to a circle with center (h, 1). Which of the following is a possible value for h if the center lies to the right of the tangent line?
whyCorrect: The radius is never given, so tangency alone puts no restriction on h - any center can be tangent to the line for the right radius. The only condition that bites is the position. Find where the line reaches the height of the center: set y = 1, so 1 = 3h − 14 gives x = 5. At the height y = 1 the line sits at x = 5, so the center (h, 1) is to the right of the line exactly when h > 5. Only 7 qualifies.

whyWrong.A: 2 is less than 5, so this center sits to the left of the line.
whyWrong.B: 3 is less than 5, so this center also sits to the left of the line.
whyWrong.C: At h = 5 the point (5, 1) lies exactly on the line y = 3x − 14, not to the right of it, and a center on the tangent line is impossible anyway.

stem: In a circle, chord RS is parallel to diameter PQ. If the length of RS is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the length of PQ and the distance between the chord and the diameter is \(2\sqrt{7}\), what is the radius of the circle?
whyCorrect: Write everything in terms of the radius r. The diameter is 2r, so \(RS=\frac{3}{4}(2r)=\frac{3r}{2}\) and half the chord is \(\frac{3r}{4}\). Drop the perpendicular from the center to the chord: it has length \(2\sqrt{7}\) and, with half the chord, forms a right triangle whose hypotenuse is a radius. So \(r^{2}=\left(\frac{3r}{4}\right)^{2}+(2\sqrt{7})^{2}=\frac{9r^{2}}{16}+28\). Then \(\frac{7r^{2}}{16}=28\), \(r^{2}=64\), r = 8. The trap is using \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the radius, or forgetting to halve the chord.

whyWrong.A: 6 is half of the chord RS once you know r = 8 (RS = 12), an intermediate value rather than the radius.
whyWrong.B: This scales the given distance \(2\sqrt{7}\) by \(\frac{3}{2}\). The chord ratio does not act on the distance; the distance and half the chord are the two legs of a right triangle, so they combine by the Pythagorean theorem, not by multiplication.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the given distance, treating \(2\sqrt{7}\) as half the radius. The perpendicular distance is a leg of the right triangle, not a piece of the radius.

stem: The ratio of the internal angles of triangle A is 1:2:3. Triangle B is an equilateral triangle with a side of 12 cm. If the area of triangle A and B are equal and the perimeter of triangle A is \(m\sqrt{2}+n\sqrt{6}\), what is the value of \(m+n\)?
whyCorrect: Angles in the ratio 1:2:3 summing to 180 are 30, 60 and 90, so triangle A is a 30-60-90 triangle with sides \(k\), \(k\sqrt{3}\), \(2k\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(k)(k\sqrt{3})=\frac{k^{2}\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Triangle B has area \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(12)^{2}=36\sqrt{3}\). Setting them equal gives \(k^{2}=72\), so \(k=6\sqrt{2}\). The perimeter is \(k(1+\sqrt{3}+2)=6\sqrt{2}(3+\sqrt{3})=18\sqrt{2}+6\sqrt{6}\), so m = 18, n = 6 and \(m+n=24\).

whyWrong.A: 6 is n on its own. The question asks for \(m+n\), and m = 18.
whyWrong.B: 12 is the side of the equilateral triangle. You get it as k if you apply the equilateral area formula \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}k^{2}\) to triangle A, but triangle A is a right triangle, so its area is \(\frac{1}{2}\) times the two legs.
whyWrong.C: 18 is m on its own. Add n = 6.

stem: The figure above shows a semicircle with the lengths of the adjacent arcs a, a + 1, a + 2, a + 3, and a + 4. If the value of x is 42, what is the value of a?
whyCorrect: Central angles are proportional to the arcs they cut off, and the five arcs make up a semicircle, so their central angles total 180 degrees. The five arcs sum to \(a+(a+1)+(a+2)+(a+3)+(a+4)=5a+10\), and \(x^{\circ}\) is the central angle belonging to the arc of length \(a+4\). So \(\frac{a+4}{5a+10}=\frac{42}{180}\). Cross-multiplying, \(180a+720=210a+420\), giving \(30a=300\) and a = 10. Check: the arcs are 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, totalling 60, and \(\frac{14}{60}(180)=42\).

whyWrong.A: With a = 7 the arcs total 45 and the last arc is 11, giving a central angle of \(\frac{11}{45}(180)=44\), not 42.
whyWrong.B: With a = 8 the arcs total 50 and the last arc is 12, giving \(\frac{12}{50}(180)=43.2\).
whyWrong.C: With a = 9 the arcs total 55 and the last arc is 13, giving \(\frac{13}{55}(180)\approx 42.5\) - close, which is why it is offered, but not exact.

note: Figure needed: a semicircle with centre O on the flat side, divided into five arcs by four radii. Going from the left end of the diameter to the right end the arcs are labelled a, a + 1, a + 2, a + 3, a + 4. The central angle of the last arc (a + 4), nearest the right end of the diameter, is labelled x degrees. Without the figure there is nothing telling the student which arc x belongs to.

stem: A right triangular pyramid has exactly six edges. Each of these edges is 96 centimeters long. If the surface area of the pyramid is \(k\sqrt{3}\) square centimeters, what is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Six edges all of the same length means all four faces are congruent equilateral triangles - a regular tetrahedron, so the base counts as a face too. An equilateral triangle of side \(s\) has area \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^{2}\), so one face is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(96)^{2}=2304\sqrt{3}\). Four of them give \(9216\sqrt{3}\), so k = 9216. The common slip is counting only the three slanted faces and getting 6,912.

stem: A right rectangular prism has a base of 28p square centimeters (cm<sup>2</sup>). The length of the base of the rectangular prism is 12 cm, and the height of the rectangular prism is 4 cm. Which expression represents the surface area, in cm<sup>2</sup>, of the right rectangular prism?
whyCorrect: The base area is length times width, so \(w=\frac{28p}{12}=\frac{7p}{3}\). Add the three pairs of faces: top and bottom give \(2(28p)=56p\); the two faces measuring 12 by 4 give \(2(48)=96\); the two faces measuring \(\frac{7p}{3}\) by 4 give \(2\cdot\frac{28p}{3}=\frac{56p}{3}\). Combine the p-terms over a common denominator: \(56p+\frac{56p}{3}=\frac{224p}{3}\), giving \(\frac{224p}{3}+96\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(\frac{224p}{3}+96p\) written as one fraction. The 96 comes from the two 12-by-4 faces, whose dimensions contain no p, so it cannot pick up a factor of p.
whyWrong.C: This uses 12 by 4 for all four side faces, giving 4(48) = 192, which would only be right if the base were a square of side 12. Only one pair of side faces uses the 12 cm edge; the other pair uses the width \(\frac{7p}{3}\).
whyWrong.D: The 96 is right but the p-term is far too large. It comes from multiplying by the base area 28p again instead of dividing it by 12 to get the width.

note: The book prints 'A right triangular prism has a base of 28p square centimeters', then calls it a rectangular prism in every following sentence; transcribed as 'right rectangular prism'. This is also the third printing of the same item - Geometry #46 (page 54), #55 (page 56) and #80 (page 60) are identical. Bank only one.

stem: A right square pyramid has a total surface area of 36,864 square inches, and the combined surface area of the four lateral faces of this pyramid is 20,480 square inches. What is the height, in inches, of this pyramid?
whyCorrect: The base area is the total minus the lateral area: 36,864 − 20,480 = 16,384 square inches, so the base edge is \(\sqrt{16{,}384}=128\) inches. The four lateral faces are triangles with base 128 and height equal to the slant height \(\ell\), so \(4\cdot\frac{1}{2}(128)\ell=256\ell=20{,}480\), giving \(\ell=80\). The slant height, half the base edge and the vertical height form a right triangle, so the height is \(\sqrt{80^{2}-64^{2}}=\sqrt{6400-4096}=\sqrt{2304}=48\).

whyWrong.B: 64 is half the base edge, the horizontal leg of the right triangle, not the vertical height.
whyWrong.C: 80 is the slant height. It is the hypotenuse of the triangle containing the height, so the height must be shorter.
whyWrong.D: 128 is the base edge of the pyramid.

stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is (9x − 490). The sum of the measures of one of the acute angles and three of the obtuse angles is (−18x + w). What is the value of w?
whyCorrect: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, all four acute angles are congruent and each obtuse angle is the supplement of an acute one. So each obtuse angle is 180 − (9x − 490). One acute plus three obtuse is (9x − 490) + 3[180 − (9x − 490)] = 540 − 2(9x − 490) = 1520 − 18x. Matching that to −18x + w gives w = 1520. You never need x - the matching −18x terms are the signal that they cancel.
note: Duplicate of Geometry #29 on page 52, except that this printing drops the degree symbols after both expressions (page 52 prints them). Bank only one.

stem: Right rectangular prism X is similar to right rectangular prism Y. The surface area of right rectangular prism X is 59 cm<sup>2</sup>, and the surface area of right rectangular prism Y is 1,475 cm<sup>2</sup>. The volume of right rectangular prism Y is 1,500 cm<sup>3</sup>. What is the sum of the volumes, in cm<sup>3</sup>, of right rectangular prism X and right rectangular prism Y?
whyCorrect: For similar solids, areas scale as the square of the linear ratio and volumes as the cube. The surface areas give \(\frac{1475}{59}=25\), so the linear ratio of Y to X is \(\sqrt{25}=5\). Volumes therefore scale by \(5^{3}=125\), so \(V_{X}=\frac{1500}{125}=12\). The sum is 12 + 1,500 = 1,512. The mistake to avoid is dividing the volume by 25 instead of 125.

stem: The figure shown is a right rectangular pyramid, where l = 18 units, w = 9 units, and h = 12 units. What is the surface area, in square units, of the pyramid?
whyCorrect: A rectangular base gives two different slant heights, one for each pair of opposite faces, and each uses half of the edge it is perpendicular to. The two faces whose base is w = 9 have slant height \(\sqrt{12^{2}+9^{2}}=15\) (using half of l = 18), contributing \(2\cdot\frac{1}{2}(9)(15)=135\). The two faces whose base is l = 18 have slant height \(\sqrt{12^{2}+4.5^{2}}=\sqrt{164.25}=\frac{3\sqrt{73}}{2}\) (using half of w = 9), contributing \(2\cdot\frac{1}{2}(18)\cdot\frac{3\sqrt{73}}{2}=27\sqrt{73}\). Add the base, 18(9) = 162: the total is \(162+135+27\sqrt{73}=297+27\sqrt{73}\).

whyWrong.B: This applies the awkward slant height to all four lateral faces, doubling \(27\sqrt{73}\), and so never produces the 135 from the pair whose slant height comes out to a whole 15. The constant term should be 162 + 135 = 297.
whyWrong.C: The radicand is wrong - the slant height for the long faces is \(\sqrt{12^{2}+4.5^{2}}\), which reduces to \(\frac{3\sqrt{73}}{2}\), not anything over 193 - and the 135 from the other pair of faces is missing again.
whyWrong.D: 324 is twice the base area, the error of counting two bases as if this were a prism. A pyramid has one base, and the second constant, 135, comes from lateral faces, not a second base.

note: The figure only labels l, w and h, all of which are given numerically in the stem, so no figure is required to answer it.

stem: A right square pyramid has a height of 11 centimeters (cm). A second right square pyramid has a height of 22 centimeters. The area of the base of each of the two pyramids is 100 cm<sup>2</sup>. Which of the following is closest to the difference in the surface area of the second pyramid and the surface area of the first pyramid, in cm<sup>2</sup>?
whyCorrect: Each base is a square of area 100, so each base edge is 10 cm and the two bases cancel out of the difference - only the lateral areas differ. The slant height uses half the base edge: \(\sqrt{11^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{146}\approx 12.083\) and \(\sqrt{22^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{509}\approx 22.561\). Lateral area is \(4\cdot\frac{1}{2}(10)\ell=20\ell\), so the difference is \(20(22.561-12.083)\approx 209.6\), closest to 209.

whyWrong.B: This uses the vertical heights 11 and 22 directly as slant heights: 20(22 − 11) = 220. The slant height runs up the middle of a triangular face and is always longer than the vertical height.
whyWrong.C: This is the difference in volumes, \(\frac{1}{3}(100)(22-11)\approx 366.7\), not surface areas.
whyWrong.D: This is the second pyramid's surface area on its own, \(100+20\sqrt{509}\approx 551\). The first pyramid's surface area still has to be subtracted.

stem: A circle is inscribed in an equilateral triangle as shown above. Point L is the center of the circle. Points A, B, and C all lie on the circle and the sides of the triangle. The perimeter of the triangle is \(90\sqrt{3}\). The length of arc AC is equal to \(k\pi\). What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Each side of the equilateral triangle is \(\frac{90\sqrt{3}}{3}=30\sqrt{3}\), and the inradius of an equilateral triangle is \(\frac{s}{2\sqrt{3}}=\frac{30\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{3}}=15\). For the arc you need the central angle ALC. A and C are the points where the circle touches the two sides meeting at vertex Q, and a radius drawn to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the side, so quadrilateral QALC has two right angles and its angle at Q is 60 degrees; the remaining angle ALC is 360 − 90 − 90 − 60 = 120 degrees. The arc is therefore \(\frac{120}{360}\cdot 2\pi(15)=10\pi\), so k = 10.
note: Figure needed: an equilateral triangle PQR with P at the top, Q at the lower left and R at the lower right, and its inscribed circle centred at L. A is the point of tangency on side PQ, B the point of tangency on side PR, and C the point of tangency on side QR. Arc AC is the minor arc, the one on the Q side that does not contain B.

Volume (cubic units)
Cylinder A\(112\pi\)
Cylinder B\(3{,}024\pi\)
The table shows the volume of two similar solids, right circular cylinder A and right circular cylinder B. The radius of right circular cylinder A is 4 units. The surface area of right circular cylinder A is \(k\pi\) square units, and the surface area of right circular cylinder B is \(n\pi\) square units, where k and n are constants. What is the value of \(n-k\)? (The surface area of a right circular cylinder with radius r and height h is \(2\pi r^{2}+2\pi rh\).)
whyCorrect: Start with cylinder A: \(\pi(4)^{2}h=112\pi\) gives h = 7, so its surface area is \(2\pi(16)+2\pi(4)(7)=32\pi+56\pi=88\pi\) and k = 88. For similar solids the volume ratio is the cube of the linear ratio: \(\frac{3{,}024\pi}{112\pi}=27\), so the linear ratio is \(\sqrt[3]{27}=3\). Surface areas scale by the square of that, \(3^{2}=9\), so \(n=9(88)=792\) and \(n-k=792-88=704\). Do not scale the area by 27; that is the volume factor.

stem: \[5x^{2}-40px+5y^{2}+70py=325p^{2}\]In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle, where p is a constant. The center of the circle is (-8, 14). If a square is inscribed in the circle, what is the area of the square?
whyCorrect: Divide by 5 first: \(x^{2}-8px+y^{2}+14py=65p^{2}\). Completing the square gives \((x-4p)^{2}+(y+7p)^{2}=65p^{2}+16p^{2}+49p^{2}=130p^{2}\), so the center is \((4p,\,-7p)\). Matching to (-8, 14) gives p = -2 from either coordinate, so \(r^{2}=130(-2)^{2}=520\). For a square inscribed in a circle the diagonal is the diameter, \(2r\), so the side is \(\frac{2r}{\sqrt{2}}=r\sqrt{2}\) and the area is \(2r^{2}=2(520)=1040\). You never need r itself, only \(r^{2}\).

stem: In triangle DEF, angle F is a right angle, point Q lies on DE, point J lies on EF, and QJ is parallel to DF. If the length of EF is 45 units, the length of FJ is 24 units, and the area of triangle DEF is 630 square units, what is the perimeter of triangle QEJ, in units?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at F, so the legs are DF and EF: \(\frac{1}{2}(DF)(45)=630\) gives DF = 28, and the hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{28^{2}+45^{2}}=\sqrt{2809}=53\), so triangle DEF has perimeter 28 + 45 + 53 = 126. Since QJ is parallel to DF, triangle QEJ is similar to triangle DEF, and the matching sides along EF give the ratio. J is 24 from F, so EJ = 45 − 24 = 21 and the ratio is \(\frac{21}{45}=\frac{7}{15}\). Perimeters scale by the same ratio: \(\frac{7}{15}(126)=\frac{294}{5}\).

whyWrong.B: This is half of 126, which is what you get by treating J as the midpoint of EF. FJ = 24 and EJ = 21 are close but not equal, and the ratio is \(\frac{21}{45}\), not \(\frac{1}{2}\).
whyWrong.C: This scales the perimeter 126 by \(\frac{7}{10}\) instead of \(\frac{7}{15}\) - the similarity ratio read off the wrong pair of corresponding sides. The side of the small triangle along EF is EJ = 21, and it corresponds to the whole of EF = 45.
whyWrong.D: 126 is the perimeter of the large triangle DEF. Triangle QEJ is the small one cut off near vertex E.

stem: What is the area, in square units, of the triangle formed by connecting the three points shown?
whyCorrect: None of the three sides is horizontal or vertical, so there is no easy base and height - use the shoelace formula on the coordinates instead: \(\frac{1}{2}\left|x_{1}(y_{2}-y_{3})+x_{2}(y_{3}-y_{1})+x_{3}(y_{1}-y_{2})\right|\). With the points in the order shown that is \(\frac{1}{2}\left|(-3)(3-(-3))+5(-3-4)+4(4-3)\right|=\frac{1}{2}\left|-18-35+4\right|=\frac{49}{2}=24.5\). If you would rather avoid the formula, box the triangle in the 8-by-7 rectangle that just contains it (area 56) and subtract the three right triangles in the corners, which come to 31.5.
note: Figure needed: an xy-grid with x from -4 to 6 and y from -4 to 10, with three plotted points at (-3, 4), (5, 3) and (4, -3). The coordinates appear only in the figure.

stem: The area of triangle ABC above is at least 48 but no more than 60. If y is an integer, what is one possible value of x?
whyCorrect: The base AC is 5 + 7 = 12 and the height is y, so the area is \(\frac{1}{2}(12)y=6y\). Requiring \(48 \le 6y \le 60\) gives \(8 \le y \le 10\), so the integer y can be 8, 9 or 10. The segment marked x is perpendicular to AC at a point 5 units from A, so the small triangle it forms with vertex A is similar to triangle ABC: \(\frac{x}{y}=\frac{5}{12}\), giving \(x=\frac{5y}{12}\). Taking y = 9 gives \(x=\frac{45}{12}=3.75\). The other allowed values are \(\frac{10}{3}\) (from y = 8) and \(\frac{25}{6}\) (from y = 10).
note: Figure needed: right triangle ABC with the right angle at C, A at the lower left, C at the lower right and B directly above C. Along AC, a vertical segment labelled x rises from a point on AC to meet AB, meeting AC at a right angle; the part of AC from A to its foot is labelled 5 and the part from the foot to C is labelled 7. The side BC is labelled y. Only y = 9 gives a terminating decimal, so 3.75 is recorded; 10/3 and 25/6 are equally valid.

stem: For triangle ABC shown, the length of AB is 11 less than the length of AC. Point D (not shown) lies on AC such that BD (not shown) is perpendicular to AC. What is the value of \(\frac{BC}{BD}\)?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at B and the hypotenuse AC is 28, so AB = 28 − 11 = 17. BD is the altitude drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse, and its length satisfies \(BD=\frac{AB\cdot BC}{AC}\) - the area of the triangle computed two ways. Substituting, \(\frac{BC}{BD}=\frac{BC\cdot AC}{AB\cdot BC}=\frac{AC}{AB}=\frac{28}{17}\). The BC cancels, so you never have to compute it (it is \(3\sqrt{55}\), which would only make the arithmetic messy).
note: Figure needed: right triangle ABC with the right angle at B, A at the top, B at the lower left and C at the lower right, with the hypotenuse AC labelled 28. The right angle and the length 28 appear only in the figure.

stem: The three points shown define a circle. The circumference of this circle is \(k\pi\), where k is a constant. What is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Two of the points share the x-coordinate 12, so the chord joining them is vertical and the center lies on its perpendicular bisector, the horizontal line y = 7. Write the center as (h, 7) and set the distances to two of the points equal: \((h-12)^{2}+3^{2}=(h-9)^{2}\). Expanding gives \(-24h+153=-18h+81\), so h = 12 and the center is (12, 7) with radius 3. The circumference is \(2\pi(3)=6\pi\), so k = 6.

whyWrong.A: 3 is the radius. Circumference is \(2\pi r\), so the coefficient of \(\pi\) is 6.
whyWrong.C: 9 is \(r^{2}\), the coefficient of \(\pi\) in the area, not the circumference.

stem: A circle has center A, and points B and C lie on the circle. Line segments BD and CD are tangent to the circle at points B and C, respectively. The measure of angle BDC is 120°. The length of line segment CD is 12 inches. What is the area of the region that is both inside quadrilateral ABDC and outside the circle, in square inches? (Round your answer to the nearest hundredth of a square inch)
whyCorrect: A radius meets a tangent at a right angle, so angles ABD and ACD are both 90°. The four angles of quadrilateral ABDC sum to 360, so angle BAC = 360 − 90 − 90 − 120 = 60°. Segment AD splits the figure into two congruent right triangles, each with a 30° angle at A, so \(\tan 30^{\circ}=\frac{12}{r}\) and \(r=12\sqrt{3}\). The quadrilateral's area is \(2\cdot\frac{1}{2}(r)(12)=12r=144\sqrt{3}\). The part of the circle inside it is the sector with central angle 60°: \(\frac{60}{360}\pi(12\sqrt{3})^{2}=72\pi\). Subtracting, \(144\sqrt{3}-72\pi\approx 249.415-226.195=23.22\) square inches.

stem: In the figure above, O is the center of the circle and AC is tangent to the circle at D. If triangle ABC is equilateral, what is the ratio \(\frac{FE}{AC}\)?
whyCorrect: Put D at the origin with AC along the x-axis, so \(A=(-\tfrac{s}{2},0)\), \(C=(\tfrac{s}{2},0)\) and \(B=(0,\tfrac{s\sqrt{3}}{2})\) for side s. The circle is tangent to AC at D, so its center is straight above D and its radius r satisfies 2r = height of the triangle, giving \(r=\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{4}\). Substituting the line AB into \(x^{2}+y^{2}-2ry=0\) gives \(4t^{2}-5t+1=0\) for the parameter t, whose roots are t = 1 (the point B) and \(t=\frac{1}{4}\) (the point F). So F is a quarter of the way from A to B, at \(x=-\frac{3s}{8}\), and by symmetry E is at \(x=\frac{3s}{8}\). Then \(FE=\frac{3s}{4}\) and \(\frac{FE}{AC}=\frac{3}{4}\).

The vertices of rectangle OABC are the center O and the point B on the circle, so the diagonal OB is a radius, 10. A rectangle's two diagonals are always equal, so AC = OB = 10. That holds no matter what shape the rectangle is.

whyWrong.B: Also far too small; \(\sqrt{10}\approx 3.16\) would fit inside a circle of radius about 1.6, not 10.
whyWrong.C: \(5\sqrt{2}\approx 7.07\) is the diagonal of a square with side 5, which is what you get by assuming the rectangle is a square whose sides are half the radius. Nothing in the problem says the sides are 5, and you do not need them.

stem: Two identical rectangular prisms each have a height of 90 centimeters (cm). The base of each prism is a square, and the surface area of each prism is K cm<sup>2</sup>. If the prisms are glued together along a square base, the resulting prism has a surface area of \(\frac{92}{47}K\) cm<sup>2</sup>. What is the side length, in cm, of each square base?
whyCorrect: With base side s, one prism has \(K=2s^{2}+4(90s)=2s^{2}+360s\). Gluing them base to base makes a single prism \(s\times s\times 180\), whose surface area is \(2s^{2}+720s\) - the two square faces that got glued are now interior and disappear, which is why the answer is less than 2K. Setting \(2s^{2}+720s=\frac{92}{47}(2s^{2}+360s)\) and clearing the fraction gives \(94s^{2}+33{,}840s=184s^{2}+33{,}120s\), so \(90s^{2}=720s\) and s = 8.

whyWrong.A: s = 4 makes the ratio \(\frac{4+360}{4+180}=\frac{91}{46}\), not \(\frac{92}{47}\). The two differ by little, so check the ratio rather than eyeballing it.
whyWrong.C: s = 9 makes the ratio \(\frac{369}{189}=\frac{41}{21}\).
whyWrong.D: s = 16 makes the ratio \(\frac{376}{196}=\frac{94}{49}\), which looks deceptively like \(\frac{92}{47}\) but is not equal to it.

stem: In the figure above, the area of triangle ABC is equal to \(2x^{2}\). What is the cosine of angle BCP?
whyCorrect: BP is the height of triangle ABC onto base AC, and both BP and AP equal x. So \(\frac{1}{2}(AC)(x)=2x^{2}\) gives AC = 4x, and therefore PC = 4x − x = 3x. Now work inside right triangle BPC, right-angled at P: the legs are BP = x and PC = 3x, so \(BC=\sqrt{x^{2}+9x^{2}}=x\sqrt{10}\). Cosine of the angle at C is adjacent over hypotenuse, \(\frac{3x}{x\sqrt{10}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(\frac{BP}{BC}\), the side opposite the angle over the hypotenuse - that is the sine of angle BCP, not the cosine.
whyWrong.C: This is \(\frac{BP}{PC}\), opposite over adjacent, which is the tangent.
whyWrong.D: This is \(\frac{PC}{BP}\), the reciprocal of the tangent. A cosine can never exceed 1, so this can be ruled out on sight.

stem: In the diagram, OB = OA, AB = BC, the measure of angle FAO is 30°, DE is parallel to AC, and AB = 58. What is the length of BE?
whyCorrect: Put F at the origin with A = (-a, 0), C = (a, 0), B = (0, b) and O = (0, t) on BF. Angle FAO = 30° gives \(t=\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}}\), and OA = OB gives \(a^{2}+t^{2}=(b-t)^{2}\), i.e. \(t=\frac{b^{2}-a^{2}}{2b}\). Setting those equal reduces to \(\tan 2\varphi=-\sqrt{3}\) for the base angle \(\varphi\) at A, so \(\varphi = 60^{\circ}\) and the triangle is in fact equilateral with every side 58. Then \(a = 29\), \(b=29\sqrt{3}\) and \(t=\frac{29}{\sqrt{3}}\), which is one third of the way up from AC to B. Since DE is parallel to AC, E sits two thirds of the way down BC from B, so \(BE=\frac{2}{3}(58)=\frac{116}{3}\).

whyWrong.B: 29 is half of 58, the answer if you assume O is the midpoint of BF and so E the midpoint of BC. O is one third of the way up, not halfway.

whyWrong.D: 58 is the whole of BC. E is an interior point of that side, so BE must be shorter.

stem: In isosceles triangle RST, SR = ST and the length of RT is 76. If \(\tan(\angle R)=\frac{2}{35}\), what is the area of triangle RST?
whyCorrect: Because SR = ST, the altitude from S meets RT at its midpoint, splitting the base into two pieces of 38. In the right triangle formed on the left, the angle at R has the altitude h opposite it and 38 adjacent, so \(\tan(\angle R)=\frac{h}{38}=\frac{2}{35}\) and \(h=\frac{76}{35}\). The area is \(\frac{1}{2}(76)\left(\frac{76}{35}\right)=\frac{5776}{70}=\frac{2888}{35}\), about 82.514. The trap is putting the whole base 76 under the tangent instead of half of it.
note: The answer is not a clean value: 2888/35 = 82.5142857..., which is longer than a real SAT grid-in accepts (it would have to be entered as 82.51). The source numbers may be slightly off - with RT = 70 the same setup gives exactly 70. Worth a human check before banking.

stem: The perimeter of an isosceles right triangle is \(48+48\sqrt{2}\) inches. What is the length, in inches, of the hypotenuse of this triangle?
whyCorrect: With leg \(a\) the hypotenuse is \(a\sqrt{2}\), so the perimeter is \(a(2+\sqrt{2})\). Set \(a(2+\sqrt{2})=48(1+\sqrt{2})\) and rationalise by multiplying top and bottom by \(2-\sqrt{2}\): the denominator becomes 2 and the numerator \(48\sqrt{2}\), so \(a=24\sqrt{2}\). The hypotenuse is then \(24\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}=48\). The perimeter is written to look as though it splits into legs and hypotenuse; it does not.

whyWrong.A: This is half of 48, which assumes the perimeter's first term is the sum of the two legs.
whyWrong.B: This is the leg length, the value you reach partway through. The hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{2}\) times it.
whyWrong.D: This reads the \(48\sqrt{2}\) term of the perimeter as the hypotenuse. If it were, the legs would sum to 48 and the hypotenuse would come out to \(24\sqrt{2}\), contradicting that reading.

stem: A real estate company offers a series of three webinars. 1,250 people attended the first webinar. 68% of the people who attended the first webinar attended the second webinar, and 32% of the people who attended the first and second webinars attended the third webinar. How many people attended all three webinars?
whyCorrect: Each percentage is taken of the group named just before it, not of the original 1,250. First to second: 0.68(1,250) = 850 people attended both the first and second. The 32% is then applied to that group of 850, not to 1,250: 0.32(850) = 272. The trap is multiplying 1,250 by 32% (which gives 400) or by 68% + 32% = 100%.

stem: \[a,\ 26,\ 29,\ b,\ 33,\ 49,\ c\]For the given data set, the data values are listed in ascending order, where a, b, and c are constants. For this data set, the mean is 36, the median is 29, and the range is 72. What is the value of c?
whyCorrect: There are seven values, so the median is the fourth one, which is b - and the median is 29, so b = 29. The mean gives the total: 7(36) = 252. Subtracting the five known values, \(a+c=252-(26+29+29+33+49)=252-166=86\). The list is in ascending order, so a is the smallest and c the largest, and the range gives \(c-a=72\). Adding the two equations, \(2c=158\), so c = 79 (and a = 7, which is indeed less than 26).

whyWrong.A: If c = 53 then a = 53 − 72 = -19, and the seven values sum to 200 for a mean of about 28.6, not 36.
whyWrong.B: 72 is the range itself, not the largest value. If c were 72 then a = 0 and the mean would be 34.
whyWrong.D: This comes from treating the listed 26 as the smallest value, giving c = 26 + 72. But a comes before 26 in the ascending list, so a is the minimum; with c = 98 the mean would be about 41.4.

stem: Data set A consists of 18 different values that have a minimum of 12, a maximum of 80, a mean of 46 and a standard deviation of 17. The values 12 and 80 are removed from the set to create data set B, which consists of 16 different values. Which of the following statements is true?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.content: The standard deviation of data set B is greater than 17.

choices.label: D

whyCorrect: Check the mean first. The two removed values average \(\frac{12+80}{2}=46\), exactly the mean of A, so removing them leaves the mean untouched: the total was 18(46) = 828, and 828 − 92 = 736, with 736 ÷ 16 = 46. That kills both mean options. For the spread, 12 and 80 are each 34 away from the mean, further than any other value in the set can be, so deleting them removes the two largest deviations while the mean stays put - the spread must shrink. Numerically, \(\sum d^{2}=18(17^{2})=5{,}202\), minus \(2(34^{2})=2{,}312\), leaves 2,890 over 16 values, a standard deviation of about 13.4.

whyWrong.A: The mean does not move at all. Removing values changes the mean only when their average differs from the set's mean, and here 12 and 80 average to exactly 46.
whyWrong.B: Same reason as A - the mean stays at 46, so it is neither greater nor less.
whyWrong.C: Standard deviation measures spread about the mean. Taking away the minimum and the maximum, the two points furthest from the mean, always reduces the spread when the mean is unchanged.

stem: The mass of object A is 450% of the mass of object B, and the mass of object A is 0.090% of the mass of object C. If the mass of object C is p% of the mass of object B, what is the value of \(\frac{p}{1{,}000}\)?
whyCorrect: Turn each percent into a decimal multiplier before doing anything else. \(A=4.5B\) and \(A=0.0009C\), so \(0.0009C=4.5B\) and \(C=\frac{4.5}{0.0009}B=5{,}000B\). Writing that as a percent, C is 500,000% of B, so p = 500,000 and \(\frac{p}{1{,}000}=500\). The two places the arithmetic goes wrong are reading 0.090% as 0.09 instead of 0.0009, and forgetting the final division by 1,000 that the question actually asks for.

stem: The mass of object A is 483% of the mass of object B, and the mass of object A is 0.069% of the mass of object C. If the mass of object C is p% of the mass of object B, what is the value of \(\frac{p}{1{,}000}\)?
whyCorrect: Convert both percents to decimals first: \(A=4.83B\) and \(A=0.00069C\). Setting them equal, \(0.00069C=4.83B\), so \(C=\frac{4.83}{0.00069}B=7{,}000B\). As a percent that makes C 700,000% of B, so p = 700,000 and \(\frac{p}{1{,}000}=700\). Watch the small percent: 0.069% is 0.00069, not 0.069, and the question asks for p divided by 1,000, not p.

stem: In a collection of items, 10% are red, 25% are green, 35% are blue, and 30% are yellow. If there are 40 green items, how many blue items are in the collection?
whyCorrect: Every percentage refers to the whole collection, so find the whole first. Green is 25% and amounts to 40 items, so the collection has \(\frac{40}{0.25}=160\) items. Blue is 35% of that: 0.35(160) = 56. Applying a percentage to the 40 green items instead of to the total is the mistake this question is built around.

whyWrong.A: This is 35% of 40 - the blue percentage applied to the green count rather than to the whole collection.
whyWrong.B: This is the number of red items, 10% of 160.
whyWrong.C: This is the number of yellow items, 30% of 160. Blue is 35%.

stem: For the positive quantities h, j, and k, 94% of h is equivalent to 47% of j, and j is equivalent to 30% of k. What percentage of k is h? (Disregard the % sign when entering your answer. For example, if your answer is 39%, enter 39).
whyCorrect: Write each statement as an equation. \(0.94h=0.47j\), and since 0.94 is exactly twice 0.47, this says \(j=2h\). The second statement is \(j=0.30k\). Substituting, \(2h=0.30k\), so \(h=0.15k\) - h is 15% of k. Notice the first relation makes j the larger quantity, which is the step people reverse.

stem: A set of five consecutive even integers is ordered from least to greatest. The sum of the first and fourth even integers is 5,860% more than the quotient of the fifth even integer and 30. The first even integer is p% less than the fifth even integer, where p is a constant. What is the value of p?
whyCorrect: Call the integers \(n, n+2, n+4, n+6, n+8\). The first and fourth sum to \(2n+6\), and the quotient of the fifth and 30 is \(\frac{n+8}{30}\). "5,860% more than" means 59.6 times as much, not 58.6 times: \(2n+6=59.6\cdot\frac{n+8}{30}\). Multiplying by 30 gives \(60n+180=59.6n+476.8\), so \(0.4n=296.8\) and n = 742, making the fifth integer 750. Check: 742 + 748 = 1,490 and \(59.6\times 25=1{,}490\). Finally, \(p=\frac{750-742}{750}\times 100=\frac{800}{750}=\frac{16}{15}\), about 1.07.
note: The answer is 16/15, roughly 1.0667 - an unusually small and untidy value for a grid-in, though it is exactly what the stated numbers give.

stem: A biologist mixed a solution that is 0.3% sodium chloride by mass with a solution that is 0.15% sodium chloride by mass to obtain a new solution, which has a mass of 80 grams and contains 0.21 grams of sodium chloride. How many grams of 0.3% sodium chloride solution did the biologist use?
whyCorrect: Track the salt, not the solution. Let x be the grams of the 0.3% solution; the rest, 80 − x grams, is the 0.15% solution. The salt each contributes must total 0.21 grams: \(0.003x+0.0015(80-x)=0.21\). That becomes \(0.0015x+0.12=0.21\), so \(0.0015x=0.09\) and x = 60. Check it: 60(0.003) = 0.18 and 20(0.0015) = 0.03, which sum to 0.21. The usual slip is writing 0.3 and 0.15 instead of 0.003 and 0.0015.

whyWrong.D: This is 80 − 0.14, the complement of choice A. It fails immediately: 79.86 grams of the 0.3% solution alone would already contain about 0.24 grams of salt, more than the 0.21 grams in the mixture.

stem: Data set A consists of 20 different values that have a minimum of 22, a maximum of 86, a mean of 54, and a standard deviation of 15. The values 22 and 86 are removed from the set to create data set B, which consists of 18 different values. Which of the following statements is true?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The mean of data set B is greater than 54.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The mean of data set B is less than 54.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The standard deviation of data set B is greater than 15.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The standard deviation of data set B is less than 15.

whyCorrect: The removed pair averages \(\frac{22+86}{2}=54\), exactly the mean of A, so the mean does not move: 20(54) = 1,080, minus 108, is 972, and 972 ÷ 18 = 54. Both mean options are therefore out. For the spread, 22 and 86 are each 32 from the mean - further than any remaining value can be - so removing them strips out the two largest deviations while the mean stays fixed, and the standard deviation falls.

whyWrong.A: The mean is unchanged; removing values only shifts it when their average differs from the set's mean.
whyWrong.B: Same reason as A - the mean stays at 54.
whyWrong.C: Deleting the minimum and the maximum, the two values furthest from an unchanged mean, always reduces the spread.

stem: A survey was conducted in Arlington to estimate the percent of adult residents who support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town. Based on the survey, it is estimated that 51% of all adult residents of Arlington support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town, with an associated margin of error of 7%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all adult residents of Arlington?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in the town is supported by more than 58% of all adult residents of Arlington.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Arlington who support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town are between 44% and 58%.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Arlington who support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town are either less than 44% or more than 58%.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in the town is supported by exactly 44% of all adult residents of Arlington.

whyCorrect: A margin of error turns a single estimate into an interval of plausible values for the whole population: the estimate plus or minus the margin. Here that is 51% − 7% to 51% + 7%, or 44% to 58%. The correct conclusion states that interval and calls the values inside it plausible - it does not claim a single exact figure or rule out the estimate.

whyWrong.A: 58% is the top of the interval, not a floor. The survey supports values as low as 44%, so it cannot say support exceeds 58%.
whyWrong.C: This has the interval inside out. The plausible values are the ones inside 44% to 58%, not outside it.
whyWrong.D: A margin of error exists precisely because the exact population percentage is unknown. Naming one exact value, and the endpoint of the interval at that, contradicts the whole idea.

stem: To determine if age and gender are related to pet ownership at his school, Mark selected a random sample of 50 male 14- to 15-year-old students from the school and a random sample of 60 female 17- to 18-year-old students from the school. For each student, he recorded the student's age, gender, and whether the student owned a pet. Which of the following provides the best explanation for why Mark cannot draw a valid conclusion from this study?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The sample sizes are too small.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The two samples are not of equal size.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Mark will be unable to tell whether a difference in pet ownership is related to age because the two age groups are too close in age.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Mark will be unable to tell whether a difference in pet ownership is related to gender because of the difference in age. Similarly, he will be unable to tell whether a difference in pet ownership is related to age.

whyCorrect: The two groups differ in two ways at once: one is male and 14-15, the other female and 17-18. If pet ownership comes out different between them, there is no way to tell whether age or gender produced the difference, because the two variables move together across the groups. That is confounding, and it is a flaw in how the groups were formed, not in how many students were sampled. To separate the effects Mark would need groups that differ in only one variable at a time.

whyWrong.A: 50 and 60 are perfectly workable sample sizes. Size is not what breaks this study.
whyWrong.B: Unequal group sizes are routine in real studies and are handled by comparing rates rather than counts.
whyWrong.C: The age groups are not too close - they are three years apart. The problem is that the age difference is tangled up with the gender difference, not that it is too small.

stem: A development company is advertising that the mean area of the apartments in a new complex is 1,450 square feet. The complex consists of 10 buildings with a total of 1,000 apartments. A sample of 50 apartments will be selected from the complex to test the company's statement about the mean apartment area. Which of the following is an unbiased sampling method?

choices.label: B
choices.content: Select the first 50 apartments that are occupied.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Select at random 5 top-floor apartments from each of the buildings.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Select at random 50 apartments from all the apartments in the 10 buildings.

whyCorrect: A sampling method is unbiased when every apartment in the complex has the same chance of being chosen. Only the last option draws at random from the whole population of 1,000 apartments. The word "random" alone is not enough - two of the wrong choices restrict which apartments are eligible before any randomness is applied, and that restriction is where the bias enters.

whyWrong.A: Order of construction is not random and may track apartment size or building type, so early-built apartments need not resemble the complex as a whole.
whyWrong.B: Which apartments fill first is related to how desirable they are, which is related to their size. This oversamples the more popular units.
whyWrong.C: This is random within a restricted group. Top-floor apartments are excluded from being ordinary units in most complexes and are often larger, and no apartment on a lower floor has any chance of selection.

stem: For which of the following sets of 9 data points is the median less than the mean?
whyCorrect: Median below mean means the data are pulled to the right by a few high values, so look for the plot with its bulk on the left and a tail stretching right. Set A has four dots at 1, two at 2 and one each at 3, 4 and 5: the fifth value in order is 2, while the mean is \(\frac{4(1)+2(2)+3+4+5}{9}=\frac{20}{9}\approx 2.22\). Median 2 is less than mean 2.22. In set B the median is 4 against a mean of about 3.44, in set C the plot is symmetric so median and mean are both 3, and in set D the median is 4 against a mean of about 3.78 - all three have the median at or above the mean.

whyWrong.B: Set B is left-skewed (1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5): median 4, mean \(\frac{31}{9}\approx 3.44\), so the median is greater than the mean.
whyWrong.C: Set C (1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5) is symmetric about 3, so the median equals the mean rather than falling below it.
whyWrong.D: Set D (1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5) is left-skewed: median 4, mean \(\frac{34}{9}\approx 3.78\).
